subject: English
description: Common one-word substitutions asked in SSC / bank exams

questions.stem: Choose the single word for 'a person who walks on foot'.

options.option_text: Pilgrim
Pedestrian
Passenger
Peddler

questions.explanation: Pedestrian — Latin 'pes / pedis' (foot). A pilgrim is a religious traveller. Passenger — traveller in a vehicle. Peddler — a door-to-door seller (also spelt 'pedlar'). Related words — biped (two-footed), quadruped (four-footed), podiatrist (foot-doctor).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the single word for 'one who loves mankind'.

options.option_text: Misanthrope
Philanthropist
Philatelist
Philosopher

questions.explanation: Philanthropist — 'philos' (love) + 'anthropos' (man). Misanthrope — hater of mankind (opposite). Philatelist — collector of postage stamps. Philosopher — lover of wisdom. Related — anthropology (study of humans), misogyny (hatred of women), misogamy (hatred of marriage).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the single word for 'a government run by a group of a few people'.

options.option_text: Monarchy
Oligarchy
Democracy
Theocracy

questions.explanation: Oligarchy — 'oligo' (few) + 'archy' (rule). Monarchy — one ruler (a king/queen). Democracy — rule by the people. Theocracy — rule by priests / by religious law. Aristocracy — rule by the nobles. Autocracy — rule by a single person with unlimited power. Plutocracy — rule by the rich.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the single word for 'one who cannot read or write'.

options.option_text: Ignorant
Illiterate
Amateur
Novice

questions.explanation: Illiterate — 'il-' (not) + Latin 'litteratus' (lettered). Ignorant is broader — lacking knowledge of a specific topic, but may still be able to read and write. Amateur — one who practises an activity without being a paid professional. Novice — a beginner in a skill or activity.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the single word for 'a life story of a person written by another'.

options.option_text: Autobiography
Biography
Memoir
Diary

questions.explanation: Biography — Greek 'bios' (life) + 'graphia' (writing) — written by another. Autobiography — life story written by the person themselves ('auto' = self). Memoir — personal narrative from a specific period of one's life; narrower than a full autobiography. Diary — daily private record.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the single word for 'one who eats both vegetables and meat'.

options.option_text: Herbivore
Omnivore
Carnivore
Insectivore

questions.explanation: Omnivore — 'omni' (all) + 'vorare' (to eat). Humans are omnivores. Herbivore — plants only (cow). Carnivore — meat only (tiger). Insectivore — insects (frog, anteater). Piscivore — fish (osprey). Frugivore — fruits (monkey). Nectarivore — nectar (hummingbird).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the single word for 'a speech made without preparation'.

options.option_text: Soliloquy
Extempore
Rehearsal
Homily

questions.explanation: Extempore — Latin 'ex tempore' (out of the time) — speech on the spot. Soliloquy — a speech character makes to themselves on stage (Hamlet's 'To be or not to be'). Homily — a sermon or moralising lecture. Rehearsal — the opposite of extempore: practising beforehand. or extemporaneous.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which single word refers to a medical specialist who diagnoses and treats disorders of the skin?

options.option_text: Paediatrician — specialist in diseases of children and infants
Dermatologist — specialist in disorders and diseases of the skin
Cardiologist — specialist in diseases of the heart and vessels
Neurologist — specialist in disorders of the nervous system

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'Dermatologist' (Greek: derma = skin + logos = study) is the term for a skin specialist. Option A is wrong because a Paediatrician treats children's ailments, not skin diseases — a common mix-up in exams since both end in '-ician'.

questions.stem: Which one word denotes the scientific study of birds, including their behaviour, classification, and ecology?

options.option_text: Herpetology — scientific study of reptiles and amphibians
Ichthyology — scientific study of fish and aquatic creatures
Ornithology — scientific study of birds and their behaviour
Entomology — scientific study of insects and arthropods

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'Ornithology' derives from Greek 'ornis' (bird) + 'logos' (study). Option D (Entomology) is the most common distractor since both are natural science branches; 'entomo' refers to insects, not birds.

questions.stem: Which one word is used for a person whose profession is to compile dictionaries and analyse the history and meaning of words?

options.option_text: Bibliographer — one who documents and catalogues books and manuscripts
Cartographer — one who designs and produces geographical maps
Stenographer — one who records spoken words using shorthand techniques
Lexicographer — one who compiles dictionaries and analyses word origins

questions.explanation: D is correct because 'Lexicographer' comes from Greek 'lexikon' (of words) + 'graphein' (to write). Option A is a trap — a Bibliographer documents books, not the words inside them. Samuel Johnson and Noah Webster are famous lexicographers.

questions.stem: Which word describes the art of producing beautifully styled and decorative handwriting using special pens or brushes?

options.option_text: Calligraphy — the art of beautiful and decorative stylised handwriting
Typography — the technique of arranging printed type for readability
Lithography — a printing technique using a flat polished stone surface
Stenography — the practice of writing speech rapidly in shorthand

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'Calligraphy' (Greek: kallos = beauty + graphein = write) specifically means beautiful decorative handwriting. Option B (Typography) is the most tempting distractor because it also relates to letters and text, but it refers to arranging printed/typeset text, not handwriting.

questions.stem: Which one word describes an extreme, irrational, and persistent fear of open spaces or crowded public areas?

options.option_text: Acrophobia — extreme irrational fear of heights and elevated places
Claustrophobia — extreme irrational fear of confined or enclosed spaces
Agoraphobia — extreme irrational fear of open or crowded public places
Xenophobia — extreme fear or hatred of people from foreign countries

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'Agoraphobia' derives from Greek 'agora' (open public marketplace) + 'phobos' (fear). Option B (Claustrophobia) is the most common wrong answer since students often swap open/closed phobias — claustrophobia is the opposite, being fear of enclosed spaces.

questions.stem: Which one word refers to the philosophical doctrine that holds the pursuit of pleasure or sensory gratification as the highest good and purpose of human life?

options.option_text: Stoicism — philosophy of enduring hardship through reason and discipline
Nihilism — doctrine that life is inherently meaningless and morality non-existent
Hedonism — doctrine that pleasure and happiness constitute the chief good
Utilitarianism — doctrine focused on maximising overall societal happiness

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'Hedonism' (Greek: hedone = pleasure) is precisely the doctrine that pleasure is life's highest good. Option D (Utilitarianism) is the sharpest distractor — it also involves happiness, but as a collective social calculus (greatest good for greatest number), not personal pleasure-seeking.

questions.stem: Which single word denotes a system of government in which the supreme authority is exercised by religious priests or clergy claiming to rule in the name of God?

options.option_text: Theocracy — government in which priests exercise power in the name of God
Plutocracy — government in which the wealthy elite hold and exercise power
Oligarchy — government in which power rests with a small privileged elite
Meritocracy — government in which rulers are chosen by demonstrated ability

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'Theocracy' (Greek: theos = God + kratos = rule) is the system where clergy govern citing divine mandate — historical examples include the Vatican and ancient Egypt. Option C (Oligarchy) is the most tempting distractor because priests form a small group, but Oligarchy does not imply religious authority — the defining element here is the divine/religious basis of rule.
